value.preferred_texture_seasoned: Deep, fertile, well-drained loam suits corn best. Its roots run deep and it feeds heavily, so a soil rich in organic matter that holds moisture through the tasseling and silking window without waterlogging gives the fullest ears.
value.preferred_texture_beginner: Corn grows best in deep, rich, well-drained soil like loam. Because it grows tall and feeds heavily, mixing in compost before planting helps the soil hold the steady moisture the plants need when the ears are forming.
value.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Sandy and clay loams both grow good corn if drainage is sound. Sandy beds warm faster and suit early sowings but dry out and leach nitrogen quicker, so they need more frequent water and sidedressing; heavier soils hold feeding longer but must be worked so they do not crust over the seed.
value.tolerated_texture_beginner: Both sandy and clay-based soils can grow corn as long as they drain well. Sandy soil warms up early but dries out and loses fertilizer faster, so water and feed a little more often. Heavier soil holds food longer but should be loosened so it does not form a hard crust over the seeds.
value.problematic_texture_seasoned: Avoid cold, wet, poorly drained ground. Corn seed, especially supersweet sh2, rots or suffers chilling injury when sown into soil below 60°F, and standing water stunts the shallow feeder roots and starves the plant of the nitrogen it needs.
value.problematic_texture_beginner: Stay away from cold, soggy, poorly drained soil. Corn seed sits and rots in cold, wet ground instead of sprouting, and standing water keeps the roots from feeding, which corn needs to do a lot of.
value.preferred_description_beginner: Corn likes deep, rich, well-drained soil. If water pools on your bed after rain, work in compost and consider a raised bed so the roots never sit wet.
value.preferred_description_seasoned: Deep, fertile, well-drained loam with compost worked in before planting. The load-bearing traits are warmth at sowing and steady moisture with high fertility through tasseling and silking.

value.note_beginner: Corn does best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, around a pH of 6.0 to 6.8. Most garden beds are already close; a soil test is the only way to know for sure and to catch soil that is too acidic.
value.note_seasoned: A soil pH of 6.0 to 6.8 suits sweet corn. Lime an acidic bed to reach that range the season before, and confirm both pH and fertility with a soil test, since corn's heavy feeding rewards a well-limed, well-fed bed.

value.timing: starter at planting; sidedress at knee-high and again at tasseling
value.notes_seasoned: Corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder. Work a balanced starter into the bed at planting, then sidedress nitrogen twice: once when plants are knee-high and again as the tassels form, the two windows when demand peaks. Sandy soils and heavy rain leach nitrogen, so split the sidedressing further where that applies.
value.notes_beginner: Corn is hungry, especially for nitrogen. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil at planting, then feed again when the plants are about knee-high and once more when the tassels appear at the top. Those are the times corn needs the most food. In sandy soil or after heavy rain, feed a little more often, since the nitrogen washes away.
value.notify_message_seasoned: Sidedress nitrogen now: your corn is at the knee-high stage where demand climbs steeply.
value.notify_message_beginner: Time to feed your corn. It is about knee-high now, which is when it needs a nitrogen boost.
value.npk_hint_seasoned: Nitrogen-forward feeding: a balanced starter, then nitrogen sidedressings at knee-high and tasseling.
value.npk_hint_beginner: Corn wants plenty of nitrogen. Use a balanced fertilizer at planting, then feed nitrogen again as it grows.
value.amount_seasoned: Follow the label rate for a heavy-feeding vegetable; a common approach is a balanced starter plus two nitrogen sidedressings.
value.amount_beginner: Use the amount on the fertilizer label for a hungry vegetable, then two lighter nitrogen feedings as it grows.

value.note_beginner: Corn is the tall centerpiece of the classic Three Sisters planting with beans and squash. The beans feed the soil the corn is so hungry for, and the squash shades the ground below. Keep corn away from tomatoes, since the two share the same ear-and-fruit worm.
value.note_seasoned: Corn anchors the traditional Three Sisters trio: beans climb it and fix nitrogen for its heavy demand, and squash sprawls below as a living mulch. The main caution is tomatoes, which share the pest Helicoverpa zea (corn earworm / tomato fruitworm), so a shared planting can concentrate it.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: The Three Sisters partner: beans pull nitrogen from the air and enrich the soil for hungry corn, and can climb the stalks.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters is the best-documented historical polyculture; the corn-bean nitrogen relationship is sound and traditional, not a crop-specific measured trial. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Pole beans use the cornstalk as a living trellis and fix nitrogen that offsets corn's heavy demand; the pairing is the well-documented Three Sisters polyculture. The benefit is soil-and-structure rather than a measured pest effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Squash
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: The third Sister: its big sprawling leaves shade the soil around the corn, holding moisture and smothering weeds.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters ground-cover role is well established and structural; foliage-diversity pest disruption is plausible but not corn-specific measured. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Squash rounds out the trio as a ground-covering living mulch that shades soil, conserves moisture, and suppresses weeds around the corn. A soil-and-space benefit; give it room so it does not swamp young corn.

good_seasoned.name: Beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The Three Sisters partner; beans fix nitrogen that helps carry corn's heavy feeding demand, and climb the stalks.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters, documented traditional Native American polyculture.

good_seasoned.name: Squash
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The third Sister; its sprawling canopy shades soil and suppresses weeds around the upright corn.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Corn and tomatoes are hit by the same worm, called the corn earworm on corn and the tomato fruitworm on tomatoes, so growing them together can build it up.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Corn earworm and tomato fruitworm are the same species, Helicoverpa zea; a shared host planting concentrates it. Sound, consistently reported mechanism; no opened controlled trial quantifying the garden effect this session. mechanistic/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Corn and tomato share Helicoverpa zea (corn earworm on corn, tomato fruitworm on tomato). Interplanting gives the pest two sequential hosts in one spot, so separating them limits the buildup.

bad_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Corn and tomato share the pest Helicoverpa zea (corn earworm / tomato fruitworm); a shared planting concentrates it.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared Helicoverpa zea host; mechanism sound and consistently reported.

value.name: Corn earworm
value.symptoms_seasoned: Chewed, frass-fouled kernels at the ear tip where a fat, striped caterpillar has fed under the husk; silks may be clipped, and tip damage opens the door to mold.
value.symptoms_beginner: A fat, striped caterpillar tunneling into the tip of the ear under the husk, leaving chewed kernels and dark droppings. It usually stays near the tip, but the damage can let mold in.
value.cause_seasoned: The corn earworm (Helicoverpa zea), whose moths lay eggs on fresh silks; the hatching larvae follow the silks down into the ear tip. It is the same species as the tomato fruitworm.
value.cause_beginner: The corn earworm, a caterpillar whose moth lays eggs on the silks. The young caterpillars crawl down the silks into the ear. It is the same pest as the tomato fruitworm.
value.organic_treatment_seasoned: Because most feeding is confined to the ear tip, the loss is often cosmetic: cut off the damaged tip at the kitchen. A few drops of mineral oil applied to the silk channel after pollination is a traditional home tactic; a spinosad or Bt product timed to fresh silks is the labeled organic option.
value.organic_treatment_beginner: The good news is the worm usually stays at the very tip, so you can just cut that part off. A classic trick is a few drops of vegetable or mineral oil on the silks after they have been pollinated, and an organic spray such as Bt or spinosad works if you time it to fresh silks.
value.prevention_seasoned: Choose varieties with tight, long husk cover, which slows the larvae, and plant early so the crop silks before peak moth flights in late summer.
value.prevention_beginner: Pick varieties with long, tight husks that make it harder for the worm to get in, and plant early so the ears silk before the moths are at their worst in late summer.

value.name: European corn borer
value.symptoms_seasoned: Small shot-hole feeding in the whorl leaves, then sawdust-like frass at leaf axils and pin-sized entry holes in the stalk and ear shank; tunneled stalks weaken and can snap.
value.symptoms_beginner: Tiny holes in the young leaves, then sawdust-like droppings where the leaves meet the stalk, and small holes bored into the stalk itself. Badly tunneled stalks can break.
value.cause_seasoned: The European corn borer (Ostrinia nubilalis), a caterpillar that first feeds in the leaf whorl, then bores into stalks and ear shanks, weakening the plant from inside.
value.cause_beginner: The European corn borer, a caterpillar that starts by chewing the young leaves, then tunnels into the stalks, hollowing them out.
value.organic_treatment_seasoned: Scout the whorls and pick off egg masses and young larvae before they bore in; a Bt product reaches them only while they are still feeding in the open whorl. Once inside the stalk they are protected.
value.organic_treatment_beginner: Check the young leaf whorls and rub out the egg patches and small caterpillars before they tunnel in. An organic Bt spray only works while they are still out on the leaves; once inside the stalk you cannot reach them.
value.prevention_seasoned: Shred and turn under cornstalks after harvest, since the borer overwinters in old stalks; rotating away from last year's patch helps too.
value.prevention_beginner: Chop up and dig in the old cornstalks after harvest, because the borer spends the winter inside them, and move your corn to a new spot each year.

value.name: Cutworms
value.symptoms_seasoned: Young seedlings clipped off at or just above the soil line overnight, often toppled and left; a gray, greasy-looking caterpillar curls up just below the surface nearby.
value.symptoms_beginner: Young corn plants cut off right at the ground overnight, as if with scissors. If you dig near a cut plant, you often find a fat gray caterpillar curled up in the soil.
value.cause_seasoned: Cutworms, the soil-dwelling larvae of several night-flying moths, which sever tender seedling stems at the base as they feed after dark.
value.cause_beginner: Cutworms, fat caterpillars that live in the soil and come out at night to chew through young stems at the base.
value.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpick at night or just under the soil around fresh damage; a cardboard or foil collar pushed an inch into the soil around each seedling blocks them.
value.organic_treatment_beginner: Go out at night with a flashlight and pick them off, or dig around a freshly cut plant to find the culprit. A little collar of cardboard or foil pushed into the soil around each stem keeps them out.
value.prevention_seasoned: Keep the bed weed-free before planting, since cutworm moths lay in weedy ground, and delay sowing until the soil is warm and seedlings grow fast through the vulnerable stage.
value.prevention_beginner: Clear weeds from the bed before you plant, because the moths lay their eggs in weedy soil, and plant into warm soil so the seedlings grow quickly past the tender stage.

value.name: Flea beetles
value.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny dark beetles that jump when disturbed, leaving fine pinholes and shot-hole pitting in the leaves of young plants; heavy early feeding stunts seedlings and can transmit Stewart's wilt.
value.symptoms_beginner: Tiny dark beetles that hop away when you get close, leaving the young leaves peppered with little pinholes. Bad early damage stunts small plants and can spread a corn disease.
value.cause_seasoned: Several flea beetle species that feed on corn seedlings; the corn flea beetle also carries the bacterium that causes Stewart's wilt from plant to plant.
value.cause_beginner: Small beetles called flea beetles that chew young corn leaves. One kind also carries the germ that causes Stewart's wilt, a corn disease, spreading it as it feeds.
value.organic_treatment_seasoned: Seedlings usually outgrow light feeding; where beetles are thick, a floating row cover over young plants (removed at tasseling for pollination) protects them, and spinosad is labeled if needed.
value.organic_treatment_beginner: Small plants usually grow past light damage. If the beetles are thick, cover the young plants with a lightweight row cover, taking it off when the tassels form so the wind can pollinate, and use an organic spinosad spray only if you must.
value.prevention_seasoned: Control weeds that harbor the beetles, plant after the soil warms so seedlings grow fast, and choose Stewart's-wilt-tolerant varieties where the disease occurs.
value.prevention_beginner: Pull weeds that shelter the beetles, plant into warm soil so the corn grows quickly, and pick varieties that resist Stewart's wilt if it is a problem where you live.

value.name: Raccoons
value.symptoms_seasoned: Ears pulled down, husked, and half-eaten overnight just as they reach the milk stage, with stalks knocked flat; damage arrives suddenly the night before you meant to pick.
value.symptoms_beginner: Ears torn open and eaten, and stalks knocked over, appearing overnight right when the corn is ready. Raccoons seem to know the exact night before you plan to harvest.
value.cause_seasoned: Raccoons, which raid sweet corn at the milk stage and can strip a patch in a night or two; they are one of the most common causes of a lost home crop.
value.cause_beginner: Raccoons, which raid ripe sweet corn at night and can clear a small patch in a night or two. They are one of the most common reasons a home corn crop is lost.
value.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no spray; exclusion is the answer. A two-wire electric fence (about 4 and 8 inches high) turned on as ears near maturity is the most reliable home defense.
value.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot spray for raccoons; you have to keep them out. A short two-wire electric fence, switched on as the ears get close to ready, is the surest way to protect the patch.
value.prevention_seasoned: Put the fence up and energize it before the ears reach the milk stage, not after the first raid, since once they find the patch they return nightly.
value.prevention_beginner: Set up and turn on the fence before the corn is ripe, not after the first raid. Once raccoons find your corn, they come back every night.

value.name: Common smut
value.symptoms_seasoned: Silvery-white galls on ears, tassels, or stalks that swell, then rupture to release a mass of powdery black spores; ear galls replace kernels and are most common on stressed or injured plants.
value.symptoms_beginner: Puffy silver-white growths on the ears or stalks that later burst into a cloud of black powder. On the ear, these galls take the place of kernels. They show up most on stressed or damaged plants.
value.cause_seasoned: The fungus Ustilago maydis, which enters through wounds and silks and is favored by hot, dry weather punctuated by injury; its spores survive years in the soil.
value.cause_beginner: A fungus that gets in through wounds and silks, especially in hot, dry spells, and forms the galls. Its spores can survive in the soil for years.
value.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no spray for the home garden; cut off and bag the galls before they rupture and blacken, to keep spores out of the soil. Do not compost them.
value.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no home spray. Cut off and throw away (do not compost) the galls before they burst, so their spores do not spread into your soil.
value.prevention_seasoned: Avoid wounding plants during cultivation, keep moisture and fertility steady to reduce stress, rotate away from infected beds, and choose more tolerant varieties where smut recurs.
value.prevention_beginner: Try not to injure the plants while weeding, keep water and feeding steady so the corn is not stressed, move your corn each year, and pick more resistant varieties if smut keeps coming back.

value.name: Common rust
value.symptoms_seasoned: Small cinnamon-brown, powdery pustules scattered on both leaf surfaces, darkening toward the season's end; heavy infection yellows and kills leaf tissue and can cut ear fill.
value.symptoms_beginner: Small rusty-brown, powdery spots on both sides of the leaves that darken later in the season. A bad case yellows the leaves and can leave the ears less full.
value.cause_seasoned: The fungus Puccinia sorghi, whose spores blow in on the wind and infect under cool, moist, humid conditions; it does not overwinter in most northern gardens but arrives each year on wind currents.
value.cause_beginner: A fungus whose spores blow in on the wind and take hold in cool, damp weather. In most gardens it arrives fresh each year rather than surviving the winter in place.
value.organic_treatment_seasoned: Most home crops tolerate rust without treatment; remove badly infected lower leaves to slow spread and improve airflow. A labeled fungicide is rarely needed in a garden.
value.organic_treatment_beginner: Most gardens can live with a little rust. Pull off the worst lower leaves to slow it and give the plants air. You rarely need to spray in a home garden.
value.prevention_seasoned: Choose rust-resistant hybrids, which are widely available, and plant early so the crop matures before rust builds late in the season; avoid overhead watering where practical.
value.prevention_beginner: Pick rust-resistant varieties, which are easy to find, and plant early so the corn is nearly done before rust gets bad late in summer. Water at the base when you can.

value.name: Stewart's wilt
value.symptoms_seasoned: Long, pale-green to yellow streaks with wavy margins running along the leaves, following flea-beetle feeding scars; severe early infection wilts and stunts seedlings, sometimes killing them.
value.symptoms_beginner: Long yellow streaks with wavy edges running down the leaves, appearing after flea beetles have been feeding. A bad early case wilts and stunts young plants and can kill them.
value.cause_seasoned: The bacterium Pantoea stewartii, carried and introduced by the corn flea beetle; mild winters that let more beetles survive drive worse outbreaks the following year.
value.cause_beginner: A bacterium spread by the corn flea beetle as it feeds. After a mild winter more beetles survive, so the disease tends to be worse the next year.
value.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy severely affected seedlings. Management is aimed at the flea-beetle vector, not the bacterium itself.
value.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure an infected plant; pull and throw away badly affected seedlings. The real control is keeping the flea beetles that spread it in check.
value.prevention_seasoned: Grow resistant or tolerant hybrids, the primary defense, and manage flea beetles on young plants with row cover or a labeled treatment to break the transmission cycle.
value.prevention_beginner: Grow resistant varieties, which is the main defense, and keep flea beetles off young plants with a row cover or an organic treatment so they cannot pass the disease along.

value.frequency_seasoned: Water regularly to keep the root zone evenly moist through the season, with the highest demand from tasseling through silking and ear fill.
value.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist. Pay the closest attention from the time the tassels appear through when the ears are filling out, which is when corn needs water the most.
value.amount_seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week from rain and irrigation, rising toward 1.5 inches per week across the pollination and ear-fill window; water deeply to wet the full root zone.
value.amount_beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, and closer to 1.5 inches while the corn is pollinating and filling ears. Water deeply so it soaks down to the roots rather than just wetting the surface.
value.method_seasoned: Deep soaking at intervals suits corn. Overhead watering is tolerated far better than on disease-prone crops, but soaker or furrow watering conserves water and keeps the canopy from staying wet.
value.method_beginner: Give corn a deep soak rather than frequent light sprinkles. Corn handles overhead watering better than many crops, but watering at the base wastes less and keeps the leaves drier.
value.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and stunted, stalled growth in ground that stays wet point to waterlogged, oxygen-starved roots.
value.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil stays soggy and the lower leaves yellow while the plant stalls, the roots are drowning. Ease off and let it drain.
value.signs_underwater_seasoned: Leaves that roll or curl at midday, especially near tasseling, signal drought stress; stress in the silking window desiccates silks and pollen and leaves gappy, poorly filled ears.
value.signs_underwater_beginner: Leaves that roll up like tubes in the afternoon mean the corn is too dry. If this happens while the tassels and silks are out, you get ears with missing kernels, so keep the water steady then.

schedule_by_stage.rate: keep the seedbed evenly moist, never soggy
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Sown into warm soil, corn wants an evenly moist seedbed until emergence, but not saturated: cold, waterlogged soil rots seed and chills supersweet sh2 kernels.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the seedbed evenly damp, not soggy, until the seedlings come up. Cold, wet soil rots the seed before it sprouts.

schedule_by_stage.rate: keep the top few inches evenly moist
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Grow young plants on with steady, even moisture while the root system establishes.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water the young plants evenly as they get their roots down.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 inch per week, wetting the full root zone
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Water use climbs steadily as the plants gain height; keep about 1 inch per week and water deeply to follow the deepening roots.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Give about 1 inch of water a week as the plants shoot up, and water deeply so it reaches the growing roots.

schedule_by_stage.rate: toward 1.5 inches per week, never let it dry
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Tasseling opens the critical-moisture window: water stress now, as pollen sheds, cuts pollen viability and the eventual kernel set. Keep moisture high and steady.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: When the tassels are shedding pollen, the corn must not dry out. Dry soil now means poorly filled ears later, so keep the water steady and generous.

schedule_by_stage.rate: toward 1.5 inches per week, never let it dry
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Silking is the single most moisture-sensitive stage: drought desiccates the silks and drops pollination, giving blank tips and gappy ears. This is where steady water pays off most.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Silking is the most important time of all for water. If the plants get dry now, the silks cannot do their job and the ears come out with gaps, so water deeply and keep it up.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Demand stays high as kernels fill; stress here aborts kernels at the ear tip rather than causing outright pollination failure. Hold steady moisture until the milk stage.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep watering steadily while the kernels plump up. Letting it dry now costs you kernels at the tip of the ear.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Keep even moisture through the short milk-stage picking window so the ears finish plump; the block ripens close together.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist through picking. The ears in a block ripen around the same few days, so steady water finishes them well.

value.method_note_seasoned: The critical moisture window is tasseling through silking and into ear fill; do not let the bed dry out then.
value.method_note_beginner: The most important time to keep water steady is when the tassels and silks are out and the ears are filling.
value.critical_periods_seasoned: Tasseling, silking, and ear fill are the moisture-critical stages; drought at silking is the single most damaging, giving gappy, poorly filled ears.
value.critical_periods_beginner: Tasseling, silking, and ear-filling are when corn most needs steady water. Drying out during silking is the worst, and leaves ears with missing kernels.

value.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Sweet corn is direct-sown in place and is not started indoors or hardened off.
value.hardening_off_beginner: You do not need to harden off corn. It is planted straight into the garden from seed.
value.notes_seasoned: Direct-sow into warm soil (at least 60°F, warmer for sh2) after the last spring frost. Corn resents root disturbance and germinates quickly in place, so transplanting offers little gain and risks setting plants back.
value.notes_beginner: Plant corn seeds right where they will grow, once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F and frost is past. Corn does not like having its roots disturbed and comes up fast anyway, so there is little reason to start it indoors.

value.room_temp_seasoned: Not recommended. Sweet corn converts sugar to starch fastest at room temperature, so hold it cold rather than on the counter.
value.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave corn out on the counter. It loses its sweetness quickest when warm, so get it into the fridge.
value.fridge_seasoned: Chill immediately after picking, husks on, to slow the sugar-to-starch conversion. Standard sugary (su) types hold good quality only 1 to 2 days, sugary-enhanced (se) a day or two longer, and supersweet (sh2) up to about a week refrigerated.
value.fridge_beginner: Cool the ears fast, leaving the husks on, and keep them cold. Old-style sweet (su) corn is best within a day or two, sugary-enhanced (se) holds a little longer, and supersweet (sh2) can keep up to about a week in the fridge.
value.freezer_seasoned: Corn freezes well for longer storage. For best quality, blanch and freeze (or can) within a few hours of picking, before the sugars turn.
value.freezer_beginner: Corn freezes well if you want to keep it. For the best flavor, blanch and freeze it within a few hours of picking, while it is still sweet.
value.notes_seasoned: Sweet corn is best eaten as soon after picking as possible. The clock is the sugar-to-starch conversion, fastest in su types and slowest in sh2: cool the ears immediately, keep them cold, and process for the freezer within hours for top quality.
value.notes_beginner: Corn is best the day you pick it. Its sugar slowly turns to starch after harvest, fastest in old-style sweet types, so cool it right away, keep it cold, and freeze it within a few hours if you want to store it.

recommended.name: Sweet G-90
recommended.note: Standard sugary (su) bicolor: classic corn flavor, but the sugar turns to starch fastest, so it has the shortest hold. Germinates in cooler soil than the sweeter types.

recommended.name: Bodacious
recommended.note: Sugary-enhanced (se) yellow: sweeter and more tender than su, holding quality a day or two longer, with no isolation needed from su types.

recommended.name: How Sweet It Is
recommended.note: Supersweet (sh2) white: holds its sweetness longest, but the seed needs warmer soil to germinate and must be isolated from su and se corn to stay sweet.

value.note_seasoned: Choose by sugar genetics. Standard sugary (su) gives classic corn flavor but the shortest quality window; sugary-enhanced (se) is sweeter and more tender and holds a little longer; supersweet (sh2) holds sweetness longest and stores best, but its seed needs warmer soil to germinate and it must be isolated from su and se types by distance or planting date, or the cross turns the kernels starchy.
value.note_beginner: Sweet corn comes in three sugar types. Standard sweet (su) tastes classic but must be eaten quickly. Sugary-enhanced (se) is sweeter and tender and holds a bit longer, and is the easiest all-around choice. Supersweet (sh2) stays sweetest the longest, but its seed needs warmer soil to sprout and it has to be kept apart from the other types so their pollen does not make it starchy.

value.when: when seedlings are 3 to 4 inches tall
value.method: snip extra seedlings at the soil line
value.tip_seasoned: If you sow thickly to insure a stand, thin within the block to a final in-row spacing of 8 to 12 inches once seedlings are a few inches tall. Snip the extras at the soil line rather than pulling, to spare the shallow roots of the plants you keep.
value.tip_beginner: If you plant the seeds close together to be sure they come up, thin them to about 8 to 12 inches apart within the block when they are a few inches tall. Cut the extra seedlings off at the ground instead of pulling them, so you do not disturb the roots of the ones you are keeping.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Not applicable. Corn is not grown in containers.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Not applicable. Corn is grown in the ground, not in pots.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Not applicable. Sweet corn is not a container crop.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Not applicable. Sweet corn is grown in the ground.

value.watering_adjustment_beginner: Not applicable. Corn is grown in the ground, not in containers.
value.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Not applicable. Corn is not grown in pots.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Corn is a warm-season annual that finishes in one season and is not overwintered.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. As a frost-tender annual, sweet corn completes its cycle in a single season and is not overwintered.

value.notes_beginner: Sweet corn is not suited to pots. It grows tall, feeds heavily, and must be planted in a block of several plants for wind pollination, so it belongs in a garden bed, not a container.
value.notes_seasoned: Sweet corn is a poor container crop: it is tall and hungry and depends on a block planting for wind pollination, none of which a single pot supports. Grow it in the ground.
value.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Not applicable. Sweet corn is not a container crop.
value.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Not applicable. Sweet corn is not a container crop.
value.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Not applicable. Sweet corn is not grown in containers.
value.self_watering_notes_beginner: Not applicable. Corn is grown in garden beds, not in self-watering pots.

value.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid following corn with corn in the same bed; rotating breaks the buildup of soil-borne diseases and corn pests, and spreads out the crop's heavy nitrogen demand.
value.avoid_after_beginner: Try not to plant corn in the same spot two years running. Moving it each year keeps corn diseases and pests from building up and gives the soil a rest from its heavy feeding.
value.good_after: Corn follows a legume well: beans or peas leave nitrogen in the soil that this hungry crop puts straight to use.
value.note_seasoned: Rotate corn on a two-to-three-year cycle and place it after a nitrogen-fixing legume where you can, since corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder.
value.note_beginner: Move your corn to a new spot each year, on about a two-to-three-year cycle. Planting it where beans or peas grew the year before gives it the extra nitrogen it wants.

value.name: Germination
value.user_action_seasoned: Sow about 1 to 2 inches deep once soil is at least 60°F (warmer for sh2), into a block of short rows. Keep the seedbed evenly moist but not saturated; cold, wet soil rots seed and chills supersweet kernels.
value.user_action_beginner: Plant the seeds about 1 to 2 inches deep once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F, laying out a block of short rows rather than one long row. Keep the bed evenly damp but not soggy, since cold, wet soil rots the seed.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare soil for roughly a week, then the coleoptile spikes through and the first blade unfurls. Emergence takes about 4 to 6 days in warm soil and much longer in cool soil. The imbibitional-chilling risk sits in the first day or two after sowing.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare soil for about a week, then a pointed shoot pushes up and the first leaf opens. Corn comes up in 4 to 6 days in warm soil, slower when it is cool. The seed is most at risk of cold damage in the first day or two after planting.
value.log_prompt_seasoned: Have your corn seedlings emerged? Note the date to track real days from sowing rather than the seed-packet estimate.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Have your corn come up yet? Write down the date you first saw the seedlings break the soil.

value.name: Seedling
value.user_action_seasoned: Keep the block evenly moist and weed-free; young corn competes poorly with weeds. Cultivate shallowly to spare the surface roots. Thin now to a final 8 to 12 inches in the row if you sowed thickly.
value.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and pull weeds early, since small corn does not compete well with them. Weed shallowly to protect the roots near the surface. If you planted thickly, thin to about 8 to 12 inches apart now.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The seedlings put out a few strap-shaped leaves and stand a few inches tall by around two to three weeks. This is the stage flea beetles and cutworms do the most harm, so watch for pinholes and clipped stems.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: The young plants send up several long, narrow leaves and reach a few inches tall by two or three weeks. This is when flea beetles and cutworms can do the most damage, so watch for tiny holes and cut-off stems.
value.log_prompt_seasoned: How is your corn stand looking? Note any gaps, thinning you did, or early insect damage.
value.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young corn plants look? Note any bare patches, thinning, or chewed leaves.

value.name: Vegetative
value.user_action_seasoned: Sidedress nitrogen at knee-high and keep moisture steady as the plants stretch up. Hill a little soil around the base for support, and hold off overhead work that could injure stalks and invite smut.
value.user_action_beginner: Feed with nitrogen when the plants are about knee-high, and keep the water steady as they shoot up. Pull a little soil around the bases to steady the tall stalks, and avoid injuring them, which can let in disease.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid upward growth from a few inches to knee-high and beyond, adding leaves and building the stalk that will carry the ears. Reproductive parts (tassel and ears) are being set inside now, so steady water and feeding here shape the crop.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: Fast upward growth from a few inches to knee-high and taller, adding leaves and thickening the stalk. Inside, the plant is already forming the tassel and ears, so steady water and feeding at this stage set up your harvest.
value.log_prompt_seasoned: How is your corn filling in? Note the height, leaf count, and any sidedressing you did.
value.log_prompt_beginner: How tall is your corn getting? Note its height and when you fed it.

value.name: Tasseling
value.user_action_seasoned: Do not let the bed dry out: this is the start of the critical-moisture window. Keep water high and steady, sidedress nitrogen again as tassels emerge, and avoid anything that knocks pollen off prematurely.
value.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady and generous now, because this begins the most important stretch for the crop. Feed once more with nitrogen as the tassels appear, and try not to shake the plants and lose pollen early.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The tassel pushes out of the top of the stalk and begins shedding pollen. This is one of the two most weather-sensitive stages: heat over 95°F or drought here kills pollen and thins the eventual kernel set.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: A feathery tassel appears at the very top of each stalk and starts releasing pollen. This is one of the two touchiest weather stages: hot spells over 95°F or dry soil now ruin the pollen and leave you with gappy ears.
value.log_prompt_seasoned: Have the tassels emerged? Note the date and any heat or dry spell during pollen shed.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Have the tassels come out at the top? Note the date and whether it was hot or dry while they shed pollen.

value.name: Silking
value.user_action_seasoned: Hold moisture at its peak: silking is the single most drought-sensitive stage. Water deeply through any heat wave, and do not disturb the block while pollen is shedding onto the fresh silks.
value.user_action_beginner: Keep the water at its highest and steadiest now, because silking is the stage that suffers most from dry soil. Water deeply through any hot spell, and leave the plants alone while pollen is landing on the fresh silks.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Silks emerge from the ear tips a couple of days after the tassel opens; each silk that catches pollen becomes one kernel. Silks stay receptive for up to two weeks. Brown, dry silks with no pollination leave blank ears.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: Silks come out of the top of each young ear a day or two after the tassels open, and every silk that catches pollen turns into one kernel. The silks can be pollinated for up to two weeks. Silks that dry up without pollen mean empty ears.
value.log_prompt_seasoned: Have the silks emerged? Note the date the first silks showed, to time the harvest about 18 to 20 days later.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Have the silks appeared at the top of the ears? Note the date, since the corn is usually ready about 18 to 20 days after.

value.name: Kernel Fill
value.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady as kernels plump; stress now aborts tip kernels rather than causing outright pollination failure. Leave the ears undisturbed and watch for raccoons as the ears bulk up.
value.user_action_beginner: Keep watering steadily while the kernels fill out. Drying out now costs you kernels at the tip of the ear. Leave the ears alone to fill, and start watching for raccoons as they plump up.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The ears bulk up and the kernels swell and fill, the husks tightening around them. The cob reaches near-full length within a week of pollination, with kernels obviously swollen by about two weeks.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: The ears fatten and the kernels swell and fill in, with the husks tightening around them. The cob reaches nearly full size within a week of pollination, and the kernels look plump by about two weeks.
value.log_prompt_seasoned: Are the ears filling? Note how plump the ears feel and when you first saw them bulking up.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Are the ears filling out? Note how full they feel and when they started to plump up.

value.name: Harvest
value.user_action_seasoned: Pick at the milk stage: browned, dry silks and kernels that run milky (not clear, not doughy) under a thumbnail. The window is only about 4 to 5 days and a block ripens together, so check daily and pull ears with a sharp downward twist.
value.user_action_beginner: Pick at the milk stage, when the silks have browned and a squeezed kernel runs a milky juice (watery means wait, pasty means too late). The peak lasts only a few days and the whole block ripens close together, so check every day and snap the ears off with a firm downward twist.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Silks brown and dry at the tip, the ear feels full and firm, and a punctured kernel runs milky. This is about 18 to 20 days after silking, and it lasts only a handful of days before the sugars turn to starch.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: The silks turn brown and dry, the ear feels plump and firm, and a poked kernel runs a milky juice. This comes about 18 to 20 days after the silks appeared and lasts only a few days before the corn turns starchy.
value.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you made your first picking? Log the harvest date and how the ears filled out.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Have you picked your first ears? Note the date and how they turned out.

value.body_seasoned: Direct-sow sweet corn after the last spring frost, once the soil is at least 60°F (warmer for sh2). Plant a BLOCK of at least four short rows, 1 to 2 inches deep, for good wind pollination.
value.body_beginner: Plant sweet corn right in the garden after the last spring frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F. Plant a block of at least four short rows, 1 to 2 inches deep, so the wind can pollinate it.

value.title_seasoned: Sow your next block of corn
value.title_beginner: Plant your next block of corn
value.body_seasoned: For a longer season, sow a fresh BLOCK about two weeks after the last, or when the first planting has three to five leaves. Stagger blocks, not single rows, so each block still pollinates itself.
value.body_beginner: To keep corn coming, plant another block about two weeks after the last one, or when the first planting has three to five leaves. Plant whole blocks, not single rows, so each one can still pollinate.

value.body_seasoned: Tasseling and silking are the critical-moisture window. Water deeply and keep the bed evenly moist; drought or heat over 95°F now gives gappy, poorly filled ears.
value.body_beginner: Your corn is tasseling and silking, which is when it needs water the most. Keep the soil evenly moist and water deeply. Dry soil or heat over 95°F now leaves ears with missing kernels.

value.title_seasoned: Start checking your corn for the milk stage
value.title_beginner: Start checking your corn every day
value.body_seasoned: About 18 to 20 days after the first silks, the ears reach the milk stage: silks browned, kernels running milky under a thumbnail. The window lasts only 4 to 5 days, so check daily.
value.body_beginner: About 18 to 20 days after the silks appeared, the corn hits its peak: brown silks and kernels that run a milky juice when you press one. This lasts only a few days, so check every day.

value.title_seasoned: Frost expected, protect or harvest corn
value.title_beginner: Frost is coming, cover or pick your corn
value.body_seasoned: Sweet corn is frost-tender and a frost kills it at any stage. If frost is forecast, cover young plants with row cover overnight; in fall, pick any ears at or near the milk stage first, since a hard frost ends the crop.
value.body_beginner: Sweet corn is killed by frost at any stage. If frost is forecast, cover young plants with row cover overnight. In fall, pick any ears that are ready or nearly ready first, because a hard frost ends the crop.

value.body_seasoned: Heat over 95°F during tasseling and silking depresses pollen production and desiccates silks, cutting the kernel set. Water deeply ahead of and through the heat to buffer the plants.
value.body_beginner: Heat over 95°F while the corn is tasseling and silking damages the pollen and dries out the silks, so the ears do not fill. Water deeply before and during the hot spell to help the plants through it.

germination.text_seasoned: Plant corn in a BLOCK, not a long single row. Corn is wind-pollinated: the tassel sheds pollen that must fall on the silks, and a block of at least four short rows (a 4 by 4 grid) fills the ears far better than one long row where pollen blows off to the side.
germination.text_beginner: Plant corn in a square block of short rows, not one long row. Corn is pollinated by wind, so the pollen from the tassels has to drift down onto the silks. A block of at least four short rows (think four rows of four) keeps the pollen among the plants, so the ears fill out with full kernels.
germination.author: plant

germination.text_seasoned: Wait for soil at least 60°F before sowing, warmer for supersweet sh2, whose tougher seed rots or takes imbibitional chilling injury in cold, wet ground. There is no head start in early planting.
germination.text_beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F before planting, and a little warmer for supersweet types, whose seeds rot in cold, wet soil. Planting early just gives you missing plants, so there is nothing to gain by rushing.
germination.author: plant

seedling.text_seasoned: Keep sweet corn away from popcorn and field corn, and isolate supersweet sh2 from su and se types by about 250 feet or two weeks' difference in tasseling. Stray pollen crosses the kernels and turns them starchy.
seedling.text_beginner: Keep your sweet corn away from popcorn and field corn, and keep supersweet types apart from the others by distance or by planting them two weeks apart. If their pollen mixes, the kernels turn starchy instead of sweet.
seedling.author: plant

vegetative.text_seasoned: Sidedress nitrogen at knee-high and again as tassels form. Corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder, and the two demand peaks are rapid stalk growth and the run-up to pollination; sandy soils call for splitting it further.
vegetative.text_beginner: Feed corn with nitrogen when it is about knee-high and again when the tassels appear. Corn is a hungry crop, and those are the two times it needs the most food. In sandy soil, feed a little more often, since the nitrogen washes away.
vegetative.author: plant

tasseling.text_seasoned: Do not let the bed dry out at tasseling. Heat over 95°F or drought as pollen sheds kills pollen viability and thins the kernel set. Keep moisture high and steady through the pollination window.
tasseling.text_beginner: Keep the soil moist while the tassels are shedding pollen. Hot weather over 95°F or dry soil now ruins the pollen, so the ears end up with missing kernels. Water deeply and keep it steady through this stretch.
tasseling.author: plant

silking.text_seasoned: Silking is the single most drought-sensitive stage: stress here desiccates silks and pollen and gives the greatest yield loss of any timing. Water deeply through any heat wave while the silks are receptive.
silking.text_beginner: Silking is the most important time of all for water. If the corn dries out now, the silks cannot catch and hold pollen, and that costs you more than dry weather at any other time. Water deeply through any hot spell while the silks are out.
silking.author: plant

kernel_fill.text_seasoned: Hold steady moisture through ear fill. Once pollination has succeeded, dry conditions show up as aborted kernels at the ear tip rather than outright failure, so keep water even until the milk stage.
kernel_fill.text_beginner: Keep watering steadily while the ears fill. After the corn has been pollinated, dry soil shows up as missing kernels at the tip of the ear, so do not let it dry out until the ears are ready.
kernel_fill.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick at the milk stage: browned silks and a kernel that runs milky under a thumbnail. The window is only about 4 to 5 days and the block ripens together, so check daily. Cool ears immediately to slow the sugar-to-starch clock.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick when the silks have browned and a squeezed kernel runs a milky juice. This peak lasts only a few days and the whole block comes ready together, so check every day. Cool the ears right after picking to keep them sweet.
harvest.author: plant

value.per_plant_seasoned: Each stalk typically yields one to two ears, which is why corn is grown in a block of many plants rather than a few; a 10-foot row returns roughly a dozen to two dozen ears over its short window.
value.per_plant_beginner: Each corn plant usually gives just one or two ears, which is why you grow a whole block of it rather than a few plants. A 10-foot row gives roughly a dozen to two dozen ears, all around the same time.
value.peak_production_seasoned: A block ripens close together over a short 4-to-5-day milk-stage window, then the sugars turn. Staggered blocks (or su, se, and sh2 types of differing maturity) spread the harvest instead of one glut.
value.peak_production_beginner: A block of corn comes ready all within a few days, then quickly goes past its best. Planting blocks a couple of weeks apart, or mixing early and late varieties, spreads out the harvest instead of getting it all at once.
value.first_year_note_seasoned: Sweet corn is rewarding but space-hungry for a first-year grower: it needs a block of several rows, steady water at silking, and protection from raccoons at the finish. Given those, a short block delivers a real harvest in 60 to 90 days.
value.first_year_note_beginner: Sweet corn is a fun first-year crop, but it needs room: plant a block of several rows, not just a few plants, keep it watered when the silks are out, and guard the ripe ears from raccoons. Do that and a small block gives a real harvest in 60 to 90 days.
factors_seasoned: Block planting for wind pollination (a single row or a few plants pollinates poorly and gives gappy ears)
Steady moisture at tasseling and silking (the critical window; drought here is the largest yield loss)
Heat during pollination (over 95°F depresses pollen and desiccates silks)
Nitrogen supply (corn is a heavy feeder; short nitrogen limits ear fill)
Raccoon and bird protection at the milk stage (a raided block can be lost in a night)

value.source_note_seasoned: No university extension or peer-reviewed source supports timing sweet corn planting by moon phase. Sow by soil temperature (at least 60°F) and your frost-free date, not by the lunar cycle.

value.label_seasoned: Ears with gaps and missing kernels
value.label_beginner: Ears with bare patches and missing kernels
value.what_happened_seasoned: The ears filled unevenly with blank patches because pollination failed on those silks. The usual causes are a too-small planting (a single row or a few plants), heat over 95°F or drought during silking that killed pollen and dried the silks, or silks that were never dusted because the block was too sparse.
value.what_happened_beginner: The ears came out with bare patches because those silks never got pollinated. This usually happens when the corn was planted in too small a group (a single row or a few plants), or when heat or dry soil during silking ruined the pollen and dried up the silks.
value.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant a BLOCK of at least four short rows so wind pollination is thorough, and keep moisture high and steady through tasseling and silking. Time plantings so silking misses the worst summer heat, and hand-shake the tassels at midday in a small planting to help.
value.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant a block of at least four short rows so the wind can pollinate well, and keep the water steady while the tassels and silks are out. Try to time it so silking is not in the hottest part of summer, and in a small patch you can gently shake the tassels at midday to spread pollen.

value.label_seasoned: Kernels starchy, tough, or not sweet
value.label_beginner: Corn came out starchy instead of sweet
value.what_happened_seasoned: The kernels were doughy and starchy rather than sweet and milky, from harvesting past the milk stage (the sugars had already converted) or from cross-pollination by nearby popcorn, field corn, or a different sugar type, which turns even a supersweet ear starchy.
value.what_happened_beginner: The kernels were chewy and starchy instead of sweet, either because they were picked too late, after the milk stage passed, or because pollen from nearby popcorn, field corn, or a different sweet-corn type drifted in and crossed them.
value.next_season_tip_seasoned: Harvest at the milk stage, checking daily once silks brown, since the window is only 4 to 5 days. Isolate sweet corn from popcorn and field corn, and keep supersweet sh2 apart from su and se types by about 250 feet or two weeks of tasseling difference.
value.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick at the milk stage and check every day once the silks brown, because the peak lasts only a few days. Keep sweet corn well away from popcorn and field corn, and keep supersweet types apart from the others by distance or by planting them a couple of weeks apart.

value.label_seasoned: Seed rotted or came up in a thin, patchy stand
value.label_beginner: Seeds rotted or came up thin and patchy
value.what_happened_seasoned: The seed was sown into soil that was too cold and wet, so it sat and rotted or suffered imbibitional chilling injury in the first day or two after sowing. Supersweet sh2, with its shrunken, tougher seed and lower starch reserves, is the most prone to a poor cold-soil stand.
value.what_happened_beginner: The seed went into soil that was too cold and wet, so it rotted or was damaged by the cold in the first day or two instead of sprouting. Supersweet types are the hardest hit, because their wrinkled seeds are weaker in cold ground.
value.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait until soil is at least 60°F at sowing depth, and warmer still for sh2; there is no benefit to early sowing. Plant into warm, well-drained ground or raised beds rather than cold, wet spots, and avoid over-watering the seedbed.
value.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F, and a little warmer for supersweet types, since planting early only rots the seed. Plant into warm, well-drained soil or a raised bed instead of a cold, wet spot, and do not keep the seedbed soggy.

value.what_happened_seasoned: The ears were pulled down, husked, and eaten, and stalks knocked flat, right as they reached the milk stage. Raccoons (sometimes birds or deer) raid sweet corn at ripening and can clear a small patch in a night or two.
value.what_happened_beginner: The ears were torn open and eaten and the stalks knocked over, right when the corn was ready. Raccoons (and sometimes birds or deer) raid ripe sweet corn at night and can clear a small patch in a night or two.
value.next_season_tip_seasoned: Exclusion is the reliable defense: put up a two-wire electric fence (about 4 and 8 inches high) and energize it BEFORE the ears reach the milk stage, since once raccoons find the patch they return nightly.
value.next_season_tip_beginner: The sure fix is to keep them out. Set up a short two-wire electric fence and turn it on before the corn is ripe, not after the first raid, because once raccoons find your corn they come back every night.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Sweet corn is a warm-season crop here, so wait to sow until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F, usually about two weeks after the last spring frost. The season is short in the coldest zones, so favor early su or se hybrids under about 70 days to maturity and stagger a few blocks rather than one late sowing. A block of short rows pollinates far better than a single long row.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold-winter regions, plant sweet corn only after the last frost, once the soil has warmed up, usually a couple of weeks past your frost date. Because summers are short, choose fast, early varieties under about 70 days so the ears ripen before fall frost, and plant in a block of short rows so the wind can pollinate it.

patches.value: Sweet corn (Zea mays var. saccharata) is a tall, frost-tender warm-season grass grown for its immature ears, picked green at the milk stage. It is wind-pollinated: the tassel sheds pollen that must land on the silks, so it is planted in a block of short rows rather than one long row. Variety choice turns on sugar genetics (su, se, sh2), which set both sweetness and how long the ears hold quality after picking. Direct-sown into warm soil, it is a heavy feeder with a critical moisture window at tasseling and silking.

Sweet corn is a tall summer grass grown for its ears, which you pick young and sweet at the milk stage. Corn is pollinated by wind, not by bees: the feathery tassel at the top drops pollen that has to reach the silks below, and each silk that catches pollen becomes one kernel. That is why you plant corn in a square block of short rows instead of a single long row, so the pollen has plenty of neighbors to land on. It likes warm soil, rich feeding, and steady water while the ears are forming.

Pick at the milk stage: the silks have browned and dried at the ear tip, the ear feels full and firm, and a punctured kernel runs a milky (not clear, not doughy) juice. This is roughly 18 to 20 days after the first silks show, and the window lasts only about 4 to 5 days.

Corn is ready when the silks at the top of the ear have turned brown and dry and the ear feels plump and firm. To be sure, peek at a few kernels and press one with a thumbnail: ready corn runs a milky juice, watery juice means wait, and thick paste means you are late. This peak lasts only a few days, so check daily once the silks brown.

Work compost or aged manure into a full-sun bed before planting; corn is a heavy feeder and roots deeply. Lay the planting out as a BLOCK of at least four short rows (a 4 by 4 grid beats one long row) so wind pollination fills the ears evenly. Keep sweet corn away from popcorn or field corn, and isolate sh2 supersweets from su or se types, since stray pollen crosses the kernels and turns them starchy.

Pick a sunny spot and mix in compost before planting, because corn is a hungry crop that grows tall. Plant it in a block of at least four short rows rather than one long row: a small square (say four rows of four plants) lets the wind carry pollen from the tassels onto the silks, so the ears fill out with full kernels instead of gappy ones. Keep sweet corn well away from popcorn or field corn so their pollen does not drift in and make your kernels starchy.
